lessons.title: Operations on Real Numbers
lessons.content:
Real numbers are all the numbers you can find on a number line. They include rational numbers — numbers that can be written as fractions, like 1/2, 0.75, and -3 — and irrational numbers like π (pi) and √2 that cannot be expressed as simple fractions.

When working with real numbers, the most important rule is the order of operations, remembered by the acronym BODMAS: Brackets first, then Orders (powers and roots), then Division and Multiplication (left to right), and finally Addition and Subtraction (left to right). For example, in 5 + 3 × 2, you multiply 3 × 2 = 6 first, then add 5 to get 11. Without this rule, people would get different answers for the same expression.

Mastering operations with real numbers is essential because they appear in every CSEC math topic — from solving equations in algebra to calculating measurements in geometry. Practice with different combinations of operations until applying BODMAS becomes second nature.
objectives: Perform operations with real numbers
Apply the order of operations (BODMAS)
concepts: Real numbers include rational and irrational numbers.
BODMAS: Brackets, Orders, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction.

experiment.description: Order of Operations Challenge: Solve a series of expressions where you must click the operations in the correct order to simplify the expression.

lessons.title: Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages
lessons.content:
Fractions, decimals, and percentages are three different ways of expressing parts of a whole. A fraction like 3/4 means 3 parts out of 4. The same value can be written as the decimal 0.75 — simply divide the numerator by the denominator. As a percentage, it's 75%, which means 75 out of 100.

Converting between these forms is a core CSEC skill. To change a fraction to a percentage, multiply by 100. To go from decimal to fraction, write the decimal over its place value (e.g., 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5). Percentage problems often appear in profit and loss, discounts, and interest calculations, so it's worth practicing until you can convert fluently in both directions.

A useful tip: remember that 'percent' literally means 'per hundred'. So 25% = 25/100 = 1/4 = 0.25. Memorizing common fraction-decimal-percent equivalents like 1/2=0.5=50%, 1/4=0.25=25%, and 1/3≈0.333≈33.3% will save you time in exams.
objectives: Convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages
Solve problems involving percentages
concepts: Fractions represent parts of a whole.
Percentages are parts per hundred.

experiment.description: Visual Fraction/Percentage Slider: A bar that you can slide to see how a fraction (e.g., 3/4) converts to a decimal (0.75) and a percentage (75%) visually.

lessons.title: Types of Numbers, Factors and Multiples
lessons.content:
Numbers are grouped into families. Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, ...; whole numbers add zero; integers include negatives as well as positives; rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers (1/2, 0.75, —3, 0.3 recurring); and irrational numbers such as π and √2 cannot be written as exact fractions. Together, the rational and irrational numbers make up the real numbers that you plot on a number line.

A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, so 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13 are prime while 1 is not (it has only one factor) and 9 is not (it is 3 × 3). Every whole number greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes, and that prime factorisation is the key to finding the highest common factor (HCF) and the lowest common multiple (LCM). For 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3², the HCF is the product of the common primes with the smaller indices, 2² × 3 = 12, and the LCM uses the larger indices, 2³ × 3² = 72.

Squares, cubes and their roots belong to this topic too: 7² = 49 and √49 = 7; 4³ = 64 and the cube root of 64 is 4. Knowing the square numbers to at least 15² = 225 and the cubes to 5³ = 125 saves time in the exam. When a question asks you to classify a number, give the most specific family that applies, and when it asks for factors of an expression, remember that factors multiply together to give it while multiples come from multiplying it by whole numbers.
objectives: Classify numbers as natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational or real
Identify prime numbers and write a number as a product of its prime factors
Find the HCF and LCM of two or three numbers using prime factorisation
Use squares, cubes and their roots accurately
concepts: Natural ⊂ whole ⊂ integers ⊂ rational; rational plus irrational gives the real numbers.
A prime has exactly two factors; 1 is not prime and 2 is the only even prime.
Prime factorisation gives the HCF (smaller indices) and the LCM (larger indices).
Squares have even-index exponents in prime factorisation; cubes have multiples of three.

experiment.description: Number Family Sort: sort a mixed list of numbers into natural, integer, rational, irrational and prime categories.

lessons.title: Indices and Surds
lessons.content:
An index (power) shows how many times a base is multiplied by itself: 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. The laws of indices let you simplify expressions quickly: when multiplying powers of the same base you add the indices (2³ × 2² = 2^5 = 32); when dividing you subtract them (5^6 ÷ 5^4 = 5² = 25); and a power of a power multiplies them ((3²)³ = 3^6 = 729).

Two special indices follow from those laws. Anything (except 0) raised to the power zero is 1, because a^3 ÷ a^3 = 1; and a negative index means a reciprocal, so 2^-3 = 1/2³ = 1/8. Fractional indices are roots: a^(1/2) = √a and a^(m/n) means the n-th root of a raised to the power m, so 16^(3/4) = (√16... written as the 4th root) cubed = 2³ = 8. Solve equations such as 2^x = 32 by writing both sides with the same base: 2^x = 2^5, so x = 5.

A surd is a root that cannot be simplified to a whole number, such as √2 or √50. Surds are simplified by removing square factors: √50 = √25 x 2 = 5√2. To add or subtract surds, simplify each one first so that like surds can be combined: √8 + √18 = 2√2 + 3√2 = 5√2. To rationalise a denominator, multiply top and bottom by the surd: 1/√3 = √3/3. Leave an exact surd in your answer when the question does not ask for a decimal.
objectives: Apply the laws of indices to simplify expressions
Evaluate zero, negative and fractional indices
Solve simple equations where the unknown is an index
Simplify surds and rationalise a denominator
concepts: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n); a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m—n); (a^m)^n = a^(mn).
a^(1/n) is the n-th root of a; a^(m/n) is that root raised to the power m.
Surds simplify by removing square factors: √50 = 5√2.

experiment.description: Index and Surd Match: match each expression with indices or square roots to its simplest exact value.

lessons.title: Standard Form
lessons.content:
Standard form (scientific notation) writes a number as A × 10^n where A is at least 1 but less than 10 and n is an integer. Large numbers have positive powers of ten: 45,000 = 4.5 × 10^4 and 6,700,000 = 6.7 × 10^6. Small numbers have negative powers: 0.00072 = 7.2 × 10^-4, because the decimal point has moved four places to the right. Count the places you move the point — that count is the index.

Multiplying and dividing in standard form uses the laws of indices. (3 × 10^5) × (2 × 10^3) = 6 × 10^8; and (8 × 10^6) ÷ (2 × 10^2) = 4 × 10^4. If the number part of your answer is not between 1 and 10, adjust it: (5 × 10^3) × (4 × 10^2) = 20 × 10^5 = 2 × 10^6. Always finish by checking that 1 ≤ A < 10.

Standard form is used for measurements that are very large or very small — the distance from the Earth to the Sun is about 1.5 × 10^8 km and the mass of a dust particle about 3 × 10^-7 kg. To compare two such numbers, compare the powers of ten first, because the larger index means the larger number. Adding and subtracting in standard form is easier if you first write both numbers as ordinary numbers, or rewrite them with the same power of ten.
objectives: Write large and small numbers in standard form
Convert numbers from standard form back to ordinary form
Multiply and divide numbers given in standard form
Compare two numbers written in standard form and order them by size
concepts: Standard form is A × 10^n with 1 ≤ A < 10 and n an integer.
Moving the decimal point left gives a positive index, right gives a negative index.
Multiply or divide the number parts, then add or subtract the indices.
If A ends up outside 1 to 10, adjust A and the index until it is inside.

experiment.description: Powers of Ten Match: match each ordinary number, from a country's population to the width of a virus, to its correct standard form.

lessons.title: Profit, Loss and Discounts
lessons.content:
A trader buys goods at a cost price and sells them at a selling price. When the selling price is higher than the cost price the difference is a profit; when it is lower the difference is a loss. Profit and loss are compared with the cost price, so percentage profit = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100 and percentage loss = (loss ÷ cost price) × 100. A discount is different: it is a reduction from the marked price, so it is always worked out on the marked price, never on the cost price.

Worked example. A vendor buys a box of oranges for $2,500 and sells it for $3,000. Profit = $3,000 — $2,500 = $500, and percentage profit = (500 ÷ 2,500) × 100 = 20%. If the same box were sold for $2,000 the loss would be $500 and the percentage loss would also be 20%. For a discount, a phone marked at $40,000 with 25% off sells for $40,000 — (0.25 × $40,000) = $30,000, which is 75% of the marked price.

Paper 02 questions often work backwards. If a shopkeeper makes 15% profit and the selling price is $4,600, then the cost price is the unknown 100%: cost price = $4,600 ÷ 1.15 = $4,000. Always decide which price is the 100% base before you calculate — cost price for profit and loss, marked price for a discount. Remember too that successive discounts are multiplied, not added: 20% then 10% off $1,000 gives $1,000 × 0.8 × 0.9 = $720, not $700.
objectives: Calculate profit and loss as amounts and as percentages of cost price
Find the selling price of an item after a percentage discount on the marked price
Work backwards to find an unknown cost price or marked price
Explain why successive discounts must be multiplied, not added
concepts: Profit = selling price — cost price; loss is the same calculation when the selling price is smaller.
Percentage profit or loss = (profit or loss ÷ cost price) × 100.
A discount is a percentage of the MARKED price; the customer pays (100 — discount)% of it.
To reverse a percentage change, divide by the decimal multiplier, for example divide by 1.15 for a 15% profit.

experiment.description: Shop Floor Match: match each buying-and-selling story (cost price and selling price, or marked price and discount) to its correct profit, loss or sale price.

lessons.title: Simple and Compound Interest
lessons.content:
When money is invested or borrowed, the original sum is the principal (P), the yearly percentage is the rate (R) and the length of the deal is the time (T) in years. Simple interest is paid only on the principal, so I = (P × R × T) ÷ 100 and the amount at the end is A = P + I. If the time is given in months, convert it to years first: 9 months is 9/12 = 0.75 years.

Worked example. $10,000 is placed in a credit union at 8% per annum simple interest for 3 years. I = (10,000 × 8 × 3) ÷ 100 = $2,400, so A = $12,400. Compound interest is different because each year's interest also earns interest: A = P(1 + R/100)^n. For the same $10,000, A = 10,000(1.08)^3 = 10,000 × 1.259712 = $12,597.12, so the compound interest is $2,597.12 — $197.12 more than simple interest.

Compound interest can be calculated for any period. If interest is compounded quarterly, each quarter earns R/4 percent and there are 4T periods, so use A = P(1 + R/400)^(4T). A negative rate models depreciation: a car worth $3,200,000 losing 12% of its value each year is worth 3,200,000(1 — 0.12)^4 after four years. Read each question for the words 'per annum', 'each year' and 'compounded' before choosing the formula, and round money to two decimal places.
objectives: Use I = PRT/100 to find simple interest, the rate, the time or the principal
Use A = P(1 + R/100)^n to calculate compound interest
Convert a time given in months or weeks into years
Decide when simple or compound interest is the correct model and use a negative rate for depreciation
concepts: Simple interest is charged on the principal only: I = (P × R × T) ÷ 100.
Compound interest is charged on the growing amount: A = P(1 + R/100)^n.
For compounding more often than once a year, divide the rate and multiply the number of periods.
Depreciation is compound interest with a negative rate, A = P(1 — R/100)^n.

experiment.description: Interest Sort: sort each savings or loan situation into simple interest or compound interest, then check the amount earned in the feedback.

lessons.title: Hire Purchase and Instalments
lessons.content:
Many people cannot pay the full cash price of a stove, a motorcycle or a sewing machine, so they buy on hire purchase (HP). With hire purchase the buyer pays a deposit at once and then a fixed instalment each month for an agreed number of months. The total hire purchase price is the deposit plus every instalment added together, and it is always greater than the cash price because the seller is charging for the use of the money.

Worked example. A generator has a cash price of $48,000. On hire purchase the buyer pays a 20% deposit and then 12 monthly instalments of $3,600. Deposit = 0.20 × $48,000 = $9,600. Instalments = 12 × $3,600 = $43,200. Total HP price = $9,600 + $43,200 = $52,800, so hire purchase costs $4,800 more than cash — an extra 4,800 ÷ 48,000 × 100 = 10% of the cash price.

Exam questions ask you to find the deposit, the deposit as a percentage, the monthly instalment, the number of payments or the extra cost compared with the cash price. Read the agreement carefully: some stores charge a late-payment penalty and some give a discount for paying the balance early. When comparing offers, work out the total each way and then the difference as a percentage of the cash price before you advise which is cheaper.
objectives: Calculate the deposit and the total hire purchase price of an item
Find the extra cost of hire purchase compared with the cash price, as an amount and as a percentage
Work backwards to find an unknown deposit percentage or monthly instalment
Compare hire purchase, cash and loan offers and state which is cheaper, with reasons
concepts: Total hire purchase price = deposit + (instalment × number of instalments).
Hire purchase costs more than the cash price because the buyer pays for credit.
Extra cost as a percentage = (extra cost ÷ cash price) × 100.
A deposit is usually a percentage of the cash price, so deposit = rate × cash price.

experiment.description: Deal or No Deal Match: match each payment plan (deposit and instalments) to its total hire purchase price and its extra cost over the cash price.

lessons.title: Taxes and Utility Bills
lessons.content:
A worker's pay is reduced by statutory deductions before it reaches the bank. Gross pay is the money earned, allowances such as pension contributions are taken off to give chargeable income, and income tax is charged in bands: a lower percentage on chargeable income up to a stated threshold and a higher percentage on the amount above it. National Insurance and education tax are also deducted, so net pay = gross pay — total deductions. Always calculate the tax on the band above the threshold separately.

Consumption tax works the other way round: General Consumption Tax (GCT) is added to the price of goods. With GCT at 15%, an item priced at $5,000 costs $5,000 × 1.15 = $5,750, of which $750 is tax. If you are given the tax-inclusive price and must find the price before tax, divide by 1.15: $8,050 ÷ 1.15 = $7,000.

Utility bills combine several charges. An electricity bill is the number of kilowatt-hours used multiplied by the rate, plus a fuel charge and a fixed service charge, and GCT on the total; water bills use banded rates per cubic metre with a minimum charge. To find the units used, subtract the previous meter reading from the present one. Add the separate charges carefully, keep decimals in line, and round the final answer to two decimal places as money.
objectives: Calculate income tax on banded chargeable income and find net pay after deductions
Add GCT to a price and recover the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive amount
Work out an electricity or water bill from meter readings, usage rates and fixed charges
Interpret a pay slip or bill and check that the figures are reasonable
concepts: Chargeable income = gross pay — allowances; income tax is charged in bands.
Net pay = gross pay — (income tax + other statutory deductions).
Tax-inclusive price = pre-tax price × (1 + tax rate); divide to reverse it.
Utility charges are the sum of usage costs, fixed charges and any tax.

experiment.description: Bill Sort: sort each line from a pay slip and a utility bill into gross pay, deduction, usage charge or fixed charge.

lessons.title: Exchange Rates and Currency Conversion
lessons.content:
An exchange rate tells you how much one currency is worth in another, for example US$1 = J$155.60. Banks and cambios publish two rates: a buying rate (what they pay you for foreign currency) and a selling rate (what they charge you for it). A customer going abroad buys foreign currency at the higher selling rate, so the rate that appears in a question is part of what you must read carefully.

Converting between currencies is a multiplication or a division. To change Jamaican dollars into US dollars, divide by the rate: J$50,000 ÷ 155.60 = US$321.34. To change US dollars into Jamaican dollars, multiply: US$250 × 155.60 = J$38,900. Keep the units with the numbers as you work so that you can see which currency you have at each step, and round money to two decimal places.

Real transactions have charges. If a bank charges 1.5% commission, the customer receives less foreign currency (or pays more local currency) than the plain conversion suggests: US$321.34 × 0.985 = US$316.52. Questions also ask you to compare two banks' rates and say which gives the better deal, or to convert through a third currency. Work out the amount both ways, show the difference and state the cheaper option clearly in a sentence.
objectives: Convert amounts between two currencies using a given exchange rate
Distinguish a bank's buying rate from its selling rate and choose the correct one
Include commission or service charges in a currency conversion
Compare two exchange offers and state which is better for the customer
concepts: To change local currency into foreign currency, divide by the exchange rate.
To change foreign currency into local currency, multiply by the exchange rate.
Buying rate < selling rate; a customer buying foreign currency uses the selling rate.
Commission reduces the amount received, so multiply by (1 — commission rate).

experiment.description: Money Changer Match: match each traveller's request to the correct amount received, using the buying or selling rate shown.

lessons.title: Insurance and Budgeting
lessons.content:
Insurance spreads the cost of an unexpected loss across many policyholders. The policyholder pays a premium, usually each year; the sum insured is the most the insurer will pay; the excess is the first part of any loss the policyholder must pay; and a claim is the request for payment after a loss. Insurers often reward a claim-free year with a no-claim discount, which reduces the next premium.

The premium is normally a percentage of the sum insured. If a house is insured for $2,000,000 at 0.6% per annum, the premium is 0.006 × $2,000,000 = $12,000 a year. When a claim is made, the excess is deducted: a theft of $150,000 under a policy with a $20,000 excess is paid as $150,000 — $20,000 = $130,000. A claim larger than the sum insured is limited to the sum insured, however great the loss.

A budget is a plan for spending income. Net income is the money actually received; fixed expenses such as rent, insurance and loan repayments stay the same each month, while variable expenses such as food, transport and electricity change. A budget balances when income equals total expenses plus savings, and a deficit exists when planned spending is greater than income. Questions ask you to complete a budget table, find an item as a percentage of income, or decide whether a new commitment such as a hire purchase instalment fits within the surplus.
objectives: Explain premium, sum insured, excess, claim and no-claim discount
Calculate an insurance premium as a percentage of the sum insured and the payout on a claim
Prepare and check a simple monthly budget of fixed and variable expenses
Use a budget to decide whether a new expense can be afforded
concepts: Premium = rate × sum insured; the excess is paid by the policyholder on each claim.
Claim payout = loss — excess, and never more than the sum insured.
Budget: income = fixed expenses + variable expenses + savings.
A deficit occurs when planned spending is greater than income; every budget figure must be traceable.

experiment.description: Budget Sort: sort each household payment into fixed expense, variable expense, saving or insurance, then balance the budget in the activity.

lessons.title: Algebraic Expressions and Equations
lessons.content:
An algebraic expression is a combination of numbers, variables (letters like x or y), and operations. For example, 3x + 2y - 5 is an algebraic expression. The parts separated by + or - signs are called terms. Terms with the same variable raised to the same power are 'like terms' and can be combined: 3x + 2x = 5x, but 3x + 2y cannot be simplified further.

Solving linear equations means finding the value of the variable that makes the equation true. The golden rule is: whatever you do to one side of the equation, you must do to the other. For 2x + 4 = 10, subtract 4 from both sides to get 2x = 6, then divide both sides by 2 to get x = 3. Always check your answer by substituting it back into the original equation.

Algebra is the language of mathematics. Once you master expressions and equations, you'll be able to solve word problems, graph lines, and tackle more advanced topics like quadratics and simultaneous equations.
objectives: Simplify algebraic expressions
Solve linear equations
concepts: Like terms can be added or subtracted.
Balancing equations: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.

experiment.description: Equation Balance Scale: Drag constants and variables (x) onto a balance scale to solve for x by keeping the scale balanced.

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations
lessons.content:
A quadratic equation is one where the highest power of the variable is 2, written in standard form as ax² + bx + c = 0. For example, x² + 5x + 6 = 0 is a quadratic. These equations can have two solutions (roots), one solution, or no real solutions.

There are three main methods for solving quadratics on the CSEC exam: factoring, completing the square, and using the quadratic formula x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / 2a. Factoring is fastest when it works — for x² + 5x + 6 = 0, find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3, so (x+2)(x+3) = 0, giving x = -2 or x = -3.

The quadratic formula always works, even when factoring doesn't. The expression under the square root, b² - 4ac, is called the discriminant. If it's positive, there are two real roots; if zero, one repeated root; if negative, no real roots. This is a common CSEC question type.
objectives: Solve quadratic equations by factoring
Use the quadratic formula
concepts: Standard form: ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
The quadratic formula: x = [-b ± sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)] / 2a

experiment.description: Parabola Explorer: Adjust sliders for a, b, and c in ax^2 + bx + c to see how the parabola shifts, widens, or narrows on a graph.

lessons.title: Linear Inequalities
lessons.content:
Linear inequalities are like linear equations but with inequality signs instead of equals: < (less than), > (greater than), ≤ (less than or equal to), ≥ (greater than or equal to). Solving them follows the same rules as equations, with one crucial difference: when you multiply or divide by a negative number, you must flip the inequality sign.

For example, solve 3x - 5 > 10: add 5 to both sides to get 3x > 15, divide by 3 to get x > 5. The solution is all numbers greater than 5. On a number line, you'd draw an open circle at 5 and shade to the right. For -2x ≤ 8, divide by -2 and flip the sign: x ≥ -4.

Inequalities appear in real-world problems like budget constraints, speed limits, and minimum requirements. CSEC questions often ask you to represent the solution on a number line or as a set notation. Be careful with the direction of the sign and remember to flip it when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
objectives: Solve linear inequalities in one variable
Represent solutions on a number line
concepts: Inequality symbols: <, >, ≤, ≥.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the inequality sign.

experiment.description: Inequality Mapper: Input an inequality (e.g., 2x + 3 > 7) and watch the solution shade automatically on an interactive number line.

lessons.title: Factorisation and Quadratic Equations
lessons.content:
Factorising is the reverse of expanding: it rewrites an expression as a product of factors. Look for the highest common factor first: 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3). If there is no common factor, check whether the expression is the difference of two squares, a² — b² = (a + b)(a — b), so 25x² — 16 = (5x + 4)(5x — 4). Expressions with four terms are often factored in pairs: ax + ay + bx + by = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (x + y)(a + b).

A quadratic trinomial x² + bx + c is factorised by finding two numbers that multiply to c and add to b: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4) because 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7. When the coefficient of x² is not 1, split the middle term: 6x² + 11x + 4 needs two numbers multiplying to 24 and adding to 11, namely 8 and 3, so 6x² + 8x + 3x + 4 = 2x(3x + 4) + 1(3x + 4) = (3x + 4)(2x + 1).

Factorising solves quadratic equations because if a product is zero then at least one factor must be zero. For x² — 5x + 6 = 0, factorise to (x — 2)(x — 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3. Always rearrange the equation to equal zero before factorising, and check your factors by expanding them mentally. In Paper 02 you gain method marks for showing the factorisation, so write both the factorised form and the roots.
objectives: Take out a common factor and factorise by grouping
Factorise the difference of two squares
Factorise quadratic trinomials of the form x² + bx + c and ax² + bx + c
Solve quadratic equations by factorising
concepts: Highest common factor first, then the pattern that fits (difference of squares, grouping, trinomial).
a² — b² = (a + b)(a — b).
For x² + bx + c, find two numbers with product c and sum b.
If a × b = 0 then a = 0 or b = 0, which gives the roots of a quadratic equation.

experiment.description: Factor Match: match each quadratic expression to its fully factorised form, then read the roots from the pairs.

lessons.title: Algebraic Fractions
lessons.content:
An algebraic fraction behaves like a numerical fraction, so the same skills apply: factorise before you cancel, and cancel only factors that multiply, never terms that are added. (x² — 9)/(x + 3) becomes ((x + 3)(x — 3))/(x + 3) = x — 3. You may not 'cancel the x terms' in (x + 3)/(x + 5), because 3 and 5 are not factors of the whole numerator and denominator.

To add or subtract algebraic fractions, first find a common denominator, exactly as you would with 2/3 + 1/4. For 1/x + 1/y the common denominator is xy, giving (y + x)/xy. For 3/(x + 1) + 2/(x — 2), the common denominator is (x + 1)(x — 2), so the numerator becomes 3(x — 2) + 2(x + 1) = 5x — 4 and the answer is (5x — 4)/((x + 1)(x — 2)).

Multiplying fractions means multiplying numerators and multiplying denominators, and dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c). Factorise wherever possible so the answer is in its simplest form. To solve an equation containing fractions, multiply every term by the common denominator to clear the fractions first: 1/x + 1/3 = 1/2 becomes 6 + 2x = 3x, so x = 6. State any value that would make a denominator zero, since the fraction is undefined there.
objectives: Simplify algebraic fractions by factorising and cancelling factors
Add and subtract algebraic fractions using a common denominator
Multiply and divide algebraic fractions
Solve simple equations that contain algebraic fractions
concepts: Factorise first; cancel factors only, never separate terms.
The common denominator of 1/x and 1/y is xy.
Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.
Multiply through by the common denominator to solve a fractional equation.

experiment.description: Fraction Simplifier Match: match each algebraic fraction to its simplest form, checking which ones cannot be simplified at all.

lessons.title: Changing the Subject and Substitution
lessons.content:
A formula links quantities, and its subject is the single letter on its own, usually on the left. Changing the subject means rearranging the formula so that another letter becomes the subject, and it is done with inverse operations, applied in reverse order and to both sides. To make t the subject of v = u + at, subtract u from both sides and then divide by a: t = (v — u)/a.

Work through the operations in the opposite order to the one that built the expression, and keep the equation balanced at every step. To make r the subject of A = πr², first divide by π to get A/π = r², then take the square root: r = √(A/π). If the new subject appears twice, collect those terms on one side and factorise: from P = 2(l + b), divide by 2 and subtract to get b = P/2 — l.

Substitution replaces each letter in a formula with a number. Given s = ut + ½at² with u = 4, a = 3 and t = 5, s = (4 × 5) + ½ × 3 × 25 = 20 + 37.5 = 57.5. Watch the signs when a value is negative and square it inside brackets: if a = —2 then a² = (—2)² = 4, not —4. Write the formula, then the substitution, then the arithmetic, and give the unit of the answer where the formula measures a real quantity.
objectives: Change the subject of a formula using inverse operations
Handle formulas in which the new subject appears more than once
Substitute numbers, including negatives and fractions, into a formula
Evaluate a formula from the CSEC formula sheet accurately and with units
concepts: Inverse operations, applied to both sides, keep an equation balanced.
Work in the reverse order to the order of operations in the formula.
If the subject appears twice, collect the terms and factorise.
Substitute inside brackets before squaring, and carry the units through.

experiment.description: Formula Rearranger Match: match each formula to the correct rearrangement for the letter requested.

lessons.title: Sets and Set Notation
lessons.content:
A set is a well-defined collection of objects. 'Well-defined' means that anyone looking at the collection can say for certain whether an object belongs to it or not: 'the students in Form 5A' is a set, but 'the tall students' is not, because 'tall' is a matter of opinion. The objects in a set are called its elements or members, and the symbol ∈ means 'is an element of' while ∉ means 'is not an element of'.

Sets are written in one of two ways. In roster (tabular) form the elements are listed inside braces: A = {2, 4, 6, 8}. In set-builder notation the rule is given: B = {x : x is an even number and 0 < x < 10}, which describes the same set. Order does not matter and repeated elements are counted once, so {2, 4, 6, 8} = {8, 6, 4, 2} = {2, 2, 4, 6, 8}. The number of elements in A is written n(A); here n(A) = 4.

The empty set, written ∅ or { }, has no elements, and it is not the same as {0}, which has one element. A set with a countable number of elements is finite, while P = {2, 4, 6, 8, ...} continues without end and is infinite. The universal set, written with the symbol ξ, contains every element being discussed in a particular problem, so the choice of universal set can change the answer. Read the defining property carefully before you list elements.
objectives: Decide whether a described collection is a well-defined set
Write a set in roster form, in set-builder notation and in words
Use the symbols ∈, ∉, n(A) and ∅ correctly
Distinguish finite sets, infinite sets and the universal set
concepts: A set is a well-defined collection; ∈ and ∉ show membership.
Roster form lists the elements in braces; set-builder form states the rule.
The order of elements and repeated elements do not change a set.
n(A) is the number of elements (the cardinal number) of A; ∅ has none and {0} has one.

experiment.description: Set or Not a Set: match each collection description to the correct set written in roster form or to 'not a set'.

lessons.title: Subsets, Universal Sets and Complement
lessons.content:
Set A is a subset of set B (written A ⊆ B) when every element of A is also an element of B. If A also has fewer elements than B, A is a proper subset of B and we write A ⊂ B. Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set, including itself.

If a set has n elements, it has 2^n subsets in total, of which 2^n — 1 are proper subsets. For A = {1, 2, 3}, the list runs ∅, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {1, 2, 3} — eight subsets, which is 2³, and seven of them are proper subsets. Listing them systematically (start with none, then each single element, then each pair, then the whole set) guarantees you miss none.

The universal set ξ contains every element under discussion, and the complement of A, written A', is the set of elements that are in ξ but not in A. If ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and A = {2, 4}, then A' = {1, 3, 5}. Notice the difference between ∈ and ⊂: 2 ∈ A says 2 is an element of A, while {2} ⊂ A says the set containing 2 is a proper subset of A.
objectives: Use the subset and proper-subset symbols correctly
List all the subsets of a set and use the rule 2^n
Find the complement of a set within a given universal set
Distinguish the relation of a single element from the relation of a subset
concepts: A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B; A ⊂ B means A is a smaller subset of B.
A set with n elements has 2^n subsets and 2^n — 1 proper subsets.
The complement A' = {x : x ∈ ξ, x ∉ A}.
Every set is a subset of itself and ∅ is a subset of every set.

experiment.description: Subset Checker: sort each statement about a small set into 'element of', 'proper subset of' or 'neither', using the same set throughout.

lessons.title: Venn Diagrams and Two Sets
lessons.content:
A Venn diagram shows how sets overlap. The rectangle stands for the universal set ξ and each circle inside it stands for a set. The region where two circles overlap contains the elements that belong to both sets, and the region inside a circle but outside the overlap contains the elements that belong to only that set. When elements are counted, the number in each region is written inside that region.

Filling a two-set Venn diagram is always done in the same order. Suppose 40 students are surveyed, 25 play cricket (C), 18 play football (F) and 10 play both. Write 10 in the overlap first. Then the 'cricket only' region is 25 — 10 = 15 and the 'football only' region is 18 — 10 = 8. The students who play neither are what is left of the 40: 40 — (15 + 10 + 8) = 7, and that 7 is written inside the rectangle but outside both circles.

Always check your work by adding the regions: 15 + 10 + 8 + 7 = 40, which is n(ξ). No element can be counted in two regions, and a zero must still be written where a region is empty so that the diagram is complete. Diagrams are usually worth marks for the correct regions as well as for the final answer, so label the circles C and F and write the numbers clearly.
objectives: Draw a Venn diagram for two sets and label the universal set
Enter the intersection first, then the 'only' regions, then the 'neither' region
Use a Venn diagram to answer counting questions about two sets
Check a completed diagram by adding all the regions
concepts: The rectangle is ξ; each circle is one set; the overlap is the intersection.
The number in the overlap is used first; 'only' regions are found by subtraction.
The 'neither' region = n(ξ) — (sum of all the other regions).
The regions must add to n(ξ) — always verify before writing the final answer.

experiment.description: Venn Region Match: match each region of a two-set survey diagram (only cricket, both, neither) to the number of students it contains.

lessons.title: Union, Intersection and Complement
lessons.content:
Sets can be combined. The union A ∪ B contains everything that is in A or in B or in both, and the word 'or' in a question usually points to a union. The intersection A ∩ B contains only the elements that are in both A and B, and matches the word 'and'. The complement A' contains the elements of ξ that are not in A, and A — B (also written A ∩ B') is the set difference: the elements of A that are not in B.

Worked example. If ξ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and B = {4, 5, 6, 7}, then A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, A ∩ B = {4, 5}, A — B = {1, 2, 3}, B — A = {6, 7} and A' = {6, 7, 8}. Notice that A ∪ B has 7 elements while n(A) + n(B) = 12, because 4 and 5 were counted twice.

That double count gives the counting formula n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) — n(A ∩ B), which is the quickest way to find a missing number when the sets are large. It also shows why (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B': an element outside the union is in neither set, so it is in both complements. Read every question twice and write the symbols down before you work with the numbers.
objectives: Find the union, intersection, complement and difference of two sets
Translate words such as 'and', 'or', 'not' and 'but not' into set notation
Use n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) — n(A ∩ B) to solve counting problems
Use a Venn diagram to check a set calculation
concepts: A ∪ B = elements in A or B (or both); A ∩ B = elements in both.
A' = elements of ξ not in A; A — B = elements in A but not in B.
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) — n(A ∩ B).
'But not' means set difference; 'not' means complement.

experiment.description: Set Operation Match: match each expression such as A ∪ B or A' to the set of elements it describes.

lessons.title: Shading Regions and Three Sets
lessons.content:
Exam questions often show a Venn diagram and ask you to shade a region such as A' ∩ B or (A ∪ B)'. Translate the symbols into words first: A' ∩ B means 'not in A and in B'. Then decide which basic areas to shade — the part of B outside A — and combine them. Shading A ∪ B first and then taking the area outside both circles is the reliable way to handle a complement of a union.

A three-set Venn diagram (sets A, B and C) is divided into eight regions. Each region has a notation: A ∩ B ∩ C is the middle region; A ∩ B ∩ C' is in A and B but not C; and A ∩ B' ∩ C' is in A only. Writing the notation beside each region before you shade keeps you from shading one region too many, which is the commonest error.

Word questions translate the same way. 'Students who study Mathematics and Physics but not Chemistry' is M ∩ P ∩ C'; 'students who study at least two of the three subjects' is the union of the three pairwise overlaps; and 'students who study neither Mathematics nor Physics' is (M ∪ P)'. Underline the words 'only', 'but not' and 'at least' as you read, because they change the region that the marks depend on.
objectives: Shade a region described by set notation on a two-set Venn diagram
Name each of the eight regions of a three-set Venn diagram
Translate words such as 'but not' and 'at least two' into three-set notation
Check a shaded region against its written meaning before finishing
concepts: Translate notation into words before shading: A' ∩ B is 'in B but not in A'.
(A ∪ B)' is the area outside both circles, inside the rectangle.
A three-set diagram has 8 regions; the central one is A ∩ B ∩ C.
'At least two' is a union of pairwise overlaps, not a single region.

experiment.description: Shade It Match: match each written description (for example 'in A and B but not C') to its correct set notation.

lessons.title: Sets in Word Problems
lessons.content:
Survey problems in the real world usually involve two sets. Start by naming them, for example S for students who own a smartphone and L for students who own a laptop, and write n(ξ) from the total number of people asked. Then take the numbers from the question and place them: the number who own both goes in the overlap, and every other figure is reduced by the overlap before it is written in an 'only' region.

Worked example. In a class of 35 students, 22 belong to the debating club (D), 18 belong to the chess club (C) and 9 belong to both. Both = 9; D only = 22 — 9 = 13; C only = 18 — 9 = 9; neither = 35 — (13 + 9 + 9) = 4. From the finished diagram you can answer any part of the question: 31 students belong to at least one club, and 4 belong to neither. The checking sum 13 + 9 + 9 + 4 = 35 confirms the diagram.

Three-set problems are filled in the same order, innermost first: the triple overlap, then each pairwise overlap, then the three 'only' regions, and finally the number outside all three circles. Words such as 'only', 'both', 'at least one' and 'neither' tell you exactly which region is wanted, and the mark scheme usually rewards the correct diagram as well as the answer. Show every subtraction, and state your final answer in a sentence that names the group asked about.
objectives: Define suitable sets and enter survey data on a Venn diagram
Work from the intersection outwards to complete every region
Answer 'only', 'at least one' and 'neither' questions from a completed diagram
Solve a three-set word problem by filling the regions from the centre outwards
concepts: Write n(ξ) from the total surveyed before filling regions.
Fill the overlap first, then subtract it from each set total for the 'only' regions.
'At least one' = union of the sets; 'neither' = the region outside all circles.
Verify the diagram by adding the regions to get n(ξ).

experiment.description: Survey Sort: sort the students in a two-club survey into the four regions of the Venn diagram, then add the regions to check the total.

lessons.title: Coordinate Geometry
lessons.content:
Coordinate geometry (or analytic geometry) uses algebra to describe points, lines, and shapes on a grid. A point is written as (x, y) where x is the horizontal position and y is the vertical. The distance between two points (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂) is given by d = √[(x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)²] — this is the Pythagorean theorem in coordinates.

The midpoint of a line segment is ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2) — just average the x-values and y-values. The gradient (slope) of a line is m = (y₂-y₁)/(x₂-x₁). A positive gradient goes uphill left to right; negative goes downhill. Parallel lines have the same gradient; perpendicular lines have gradients that multiply to -1.

The equation of a straight line is y = mx + c, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). Given two points, you can find m first, then substitute one point to find c. CSEC questions often ask for the equation of a line, the gradient, intercepts, or whether points are collinear.
objectives: Find the gradient of a straight line
Determine the equation of a straight line
concepts: Gradient (m) = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1).
Equation of a line: y = mx + c.

experiment.description: Line Lab: Plot y=mx+b with draggable sliders for m and b. Show the line updating in real-time with the equation displayed.

lessons.title: Introduction to Functions
lessons.content:
A function is a mathematical relationship where each input (x) corresponds to exactly one output (y). We use the notation f(x) to represent the value of the function at x. Think of it as a machine: you drop a number in, the machine performs a specific rule, and one result comes out. If an input could lead to two different outputs, it is a relation but not a function.

Evaluating functions involve substituting a specific value for x into the rule. For example, if f(x) = 2x + 3, then f(5) = 2(5) + 3 = 13. Composite functions like f(g(x)) mean you first apply the function g, and then use that result as the input for f. Inverse functions, denoted f⁻¹(x), effectively 'undo' the original function, mapping the output back to the input.

To find the inverse of a linear function, replace f(x) with y, swap x and y, and then solve for the new y. Functions are fundamental to higher mathematics and are frequently tested in CSEC Paper 2, often requiring you to evaluate composites or determine inverse rules.
objectives: Understand function notation f(x)
Evaluate composite and inverse functions
concepts: A function maps an input to a unique output.
Inverse function f^-1(x) reverses the mapping.

experiment.description: Function Machine: Drop a number into a 'machine' that applies f(x) and g(x) to show composite functions visually.

lessons.title: Graphs of Linear and Quadratic Functions
lessons.content:
The graph of y = mx + c is a straight line: m is the gradient (how steeply it rises) and c is the intercept on the y-axis. Gradient is calculated as rise ÷ run between two points, m = (y² — y₁)/(x² — x₁), and a negative gradient slopes downwards. To draw the line, make a table of values for at least three points, or plot c and then step along by the gradient.

The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola: it opens upwards when a is positive and downwards when a is negative. It is symmetrical about a vertical line through its turning point, and it crosses the x-axis at the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0. Build a table of values covering the turning point — the middle value is the axis of symmetry — then join the points with a smooth curve, not straight segments.

Graphs answer equations that algebra alone makes slow. To solve x² — 2x — 3 = 0 graphically, read the x-values where the curve cuts the x-axis: x = —1 and x = 3. To solve simultaneous equations, plot both lines and read the coordinates where they cross. Read values from the graph as accurately as you can (half a small square), and always label the axes, the scale and the curve.
objectives: Find the gradient and y-intercept of a straight line and draw its graph
Complete a table of values and draw the graph of a quadratic function
Read the roots and turning point of a quadratic from its graph
Use graphs to solve equations and simultaneous equations approximately
concepts: y = mx + c has gradient m and intercept c; m = rise/run.
y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola, opening up when a > 0 and down when a < 0.
Roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis; the turning point lies on the axis of symmetry.
The solution of simultaneous equations is the point where the graphs intersect.

experiment.description: Graph Match: match each linear or quadratic equation to its graph and to its gradient, intercepts or turning point.

lessons.title: Pythagoras' Theorem
lessons.content:
Pythagoras' Theorem is a fundamental principle in geometry that relates the lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle. It states that the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. This is expressed as the famous formula: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse.

The hypotenuse is always the longest side of a right-angled triangle. If you know the lengths of any two sides, you can use the theorem to find the third. For example, if the two shorter sides are 3cm and 4cm, then 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25. Since c² = 25, the hypotenuse c = √25 = 5cm.

In CSEC exams, Pythagoras' Theorem is often applied to real-world scenarios, such as finding the height of a ladder leaning against a wall or the distance across a rectangular field. It is also a building block for trigonometry and coordinate geometry. Remember: this theorem *only* applies to right-angled triangles!
objectives: Apply Pythagoras' theorem to find missing sides of right-angled triangles
concepts: In a right-angled triangle: a^2 + b^2 = c^2, where c is the hypotenuse.

experiment.description: Pythagoras Visualizer: Drag the vertices of a right-angled triangle and see the squares of the sides (a^2, b^2, c^2) update in real-time to satisfy the theorem.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Ratios (SOH CAH TOA)
lessons.content:
Trigonometry is the study of the relationships between the angles and sides of triangles. For right-angled triangles, we use three primary ratios: Sine (sin), Cosine (cos), and Tangent (tan). These are easily remembered using the acronym SOH CAH TOA.

SOH stands for Sin θ = Opposite / Hypotenuse. CAH stands for Cos θ = Adjacent / Hypotenuse. TOA stands for Tan θ = Opposite / Adjacent. The 'Opposite' side is the one across from the angle θ you are using, the 'Adjacent' side is the one next to it (that isn't the hypotenuse), and the 'Hypotenuse' is always the longest side across from the 90-degree angle.

You can use these ratios to find missing side lengths or missing angles. When finding an angle, you'll need the 'inverse' functions on your calculator (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, or tan⁻¹). Trigonometry is essential for fields like navigation, construction, and engineering. In CSEC, you'll often encounter problems involving angles of elevation and depression, which require careful labeling of the triangle before applying the correct ratio.
objectives: Define sine, cosine, and tangent ratios
Use trig ratios to find angles and sides
concepts: SOH: Sin = Opposite / Hypotenuse
CAH: Cos = Adjacent / Hypotenuse
TOA: Tan = Opposite / Adjacent

experiment.description: Unit Circle Explorer: Move a point around a circle to see how the sine and cosine values relate to the coordinates of the point.

lessons.title: Angles and Polygons
lessons.content:
Most angle questions are solved from a small set of facts. Angles on a straight line add to 180° and angles at a point add to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal. When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal and co-interior (allied) angles add to 180°. Identify the fact you are using and, in a proof question, write the reason beside each step.

In any triangle the three interior angles add to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Any quadrilateral has interior angles adding to 360°. For a polygon with n sides, the interior angles add to (n — 2) × 180°, and the exterior angles always add to 360° whatever the number of sides. A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles, so each exterior angle is 360°/n and each interior angle is 180° — 360°/n.

Worked example. A regular polygon has 12 sides: each exterior angle is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°, so each interior angle is 180° — 30° = 150°, and the interior angles total (12 — 2) × 180° = 1800°, which agrees with 12 × 150° = 1800°. These facts also explain why regular hexagons, squares and equilateral triangles tile a floor: their interior angles divide exactly into 360°.
objectives: Use the angle facts for straight lines, points, parallel lines and triangles
Find interior and exterior angles of polygons using (n — 2) × 180° and 360°/n
Calculate angles in a regular polygon and decide whether a shape will tessellate
Give a reason for each step in an angle calculation
concepts: Straight line 180°, point 360°, parallel-line facts: corresponding and alternate equal, co-interior summing to 180°.
Triangle interior angles 180°; exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles.
Polygon interior angle sum = (n — 2) × 180°; exterior angle sum = 360°.
Regular polygon: each exterior angle = 360°/n, each interior angle = 180° — 360°/n.

experiment.description: Angle Facts Sort: sort each angle statement into straight line, point, parallel lines, triangle or polygon, with the numerical fact it gives.

lessons.title: Circle Theorems
lessons.content:
Circle theorems are used to find unknown angles and to prove results. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle; the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc; and angles in the same segment (subtended by the same arc) are equal. A cyclic quadrilateral has opposite angles that add to 180°, and its exterior angle equals the opposite interior angle.

Tangent facts go with the others. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact, so a radius and tangent meeting at a circle create a right angle; two tangents drawn from the same external point are equal in length and the line from the centre to that point bisects the angle between them; and the alternate segment theorem says the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.

Worked example. In a circle centre O, angle AOB at the centre is 130° and C is a point on the major arc. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc, so angle ACB = 130° ÷ 2 = 65°. Each answer needs a reason: write 'angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference' or 'angle in a semicircle = 90°' beside the value, because examination mark schemes award the reason separately. Set out the work as a short chain of deductions from the given angles to the one asked for.
objectives: Use the angle in a semicircle and the angle at the centre theorem
Apply the equal-angles-in-the-same-segment and cyclic quadrilateral facts
Use tangent and radius, equal tangents and the alternate segment theorem
Give the correct name of the theorem used for every deduction
concepts: Angle in a semicircle = 90°; angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference on the same arc.
Angles in the same segment are equal; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°.
Tangent ⊥ radius at the point of contact; tangents from an external point are equal.
Alternate segment theorem: angle between tangent and chord = angle in the alternate segment.

experiment.description: Circle Theorem Match: match each given angle fact in a circle diagram to the theorem that justifies it.

lessons.title: Introduction to Vectors
lessons.content:
A vector is a quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction. This distinguishes it from a 'scalar', which only has magnitude (like temperature or mass). Examples of vectors include displacement, velocity, and force. In mathematics, we often represent a vector as a directed line segment — an arrow pointing from one point to another.

In coordinate form, vectors are often written as column matrices, such as [x; y], where x represents the horizontal displacement and y represents the vertical displacement. To add two vectors, you simply add their corresponding components. Geometrically, this corresponds to placing the vectors 'head-to-tail' — the resultant vector is the one that goes from the start of the first to the end of the second.

Multiplying a vector by a scalar (a regular number) changes its magnitude and can reverse its direction if the scalar is negative, but it doesn't change the vector's orientation. Vectors are a powerful tool for solving problems involving movement and forces, and they appear regularly in CSEC Paper 1 and Paper 2.
objectives: Represent vectors as column matrices
Add and subtract vectors
concepts: Vectors have magnitude and direction.
Addition follows the triangle or parallelogram law.

experiment.description: Vector Tug-of-War: Drag two vectors (arrows) on a grid to see their resultant vector update as they are added.

lessons.title: Matrices and Determinants
lessons.content:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. The size or 'order' of a matrix is given as (rows × columns). For example, a 2×3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns. Matrices allow us to organize data and perform complex transformations on coordinates and systems of equations.

Matrix multiplication is a specific process where you multiply the elements of the rows of the first matrix by the columns of the second and sum them up. Because of this, you can only multiply two matrices if the number of columns in the first matches the number of rows in the second. For 2×2 matrices, the determinant is a single number calculated as (ad - bc).

The determinant is crucial because it tells us if a matrix has an inverse. If the determinant is zero, the matrix is 'singular' and has no inverse. Otherwise, the inverse matrix can be used to solve systems of linear equations. CSEC questions typically focus on 2×2 matrices, requiring you to perform basic operations, find determinants, and calculate inverses.
objectives: Perform matrix multiplication
Calculate the determinant and inverse of a 2x2 matrix
concepts: Matrix multiplication: row by column.
Determinant of [a b; c d] is ad - bc.

experiment.description: Shape Shifter: Apply a 2x2 matrix to a square on a grid and watch the square undergo rotation, scaling, or shearing based on the matrix values.

lessons.title: Transformations
lessons.content:
A transformation moves a shape on the coordinate plane. In a reflection, every point of the object is the same distance from the mirror line on the opposite side; the mirror line may be the x-axis, the y-axis or a line such as y = x. In a rotation, the shape turns through a given angle, usually 90°, 180° or 270° clockwise or anticlockwise, about a fixed centre. In a translation, every point moves by the same column vector such as (3 over —2), so the shape keeps its orientation.

An enlargement changes size. The scale factor k multiplies the distance of every point from the centre of enlargement, so a scale factor of 2 doubles all lengths and a negative scale factor (for example —1) produces an image on the other side of the centre, rotated through 180°. Area is affected by the square of the scale factor: images under an enlargement of scale factor 3 have nine times the area of the object.

To describe a transformation fully you must name its type and its details: reflection — the mirror line; rotation — the angle, direction and centre; translation — the column vector; enlargement — the scale factor and the centre. Points on the mirror line are invariant (they do not move), as are points at the centre of a rotation and the centre of an enlargement. Combined transformations are performed in the order given, and for shapes, actually tracing the coordinates on squared paper is the safest way to avoid a slip.
objectives: Perform and identify reflections, rotations and translations on the coordinate plane
Enlarge a shape from a given centre using positive, fractional or negative scale factors
Describe a transformation completely, naming its centre, line, vector or scale factor
State the invariant points and the effect of an enlargement on area
concepts: Reflection: mirror line; rotation: centre, angle, direction; translation: column vector.
Enlargement: centre and scale factor; area scales by the square of the scale factor.
Negative scale factors place the image on the other side of the centre of enlargement.
Invariant points lie on the mirror line or at the centre of a rotation or enlargement.

experiment.description: Transformation Match: match each statement of a transformation to the correct image coordinates of a point.

lessons.title: Measures of Central Tendency
lessons.content:
Measures of central tendency are numbers that represent the 'center' or typical value of a data set. The three most common measures are the mean, the median, and the mode. Each gives a different perspective on the data and is useful in different situations.

The Mean is the average — add all the values together and divide by the number of values. The Median is the middle value when the data is arranged in order from smallest to largest. If there's an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle numbers. The Mode is simply the value that appears most frequently in the set.

For example, in the set {2, 3, 3, 5, 7}, the mean is 4, the median is 3, and the mode is 3. In CSEC exams, you may be asked to calculate these for raw data or from frequency tables. Understanding which measure to use is also important — for instance, the median is often better than the mean for describing incomes because it isn't skewed by a few extremely high values.
objectives: Calculate mean, median, and mode for raw and grouped data
concepts: Mean: sum of values / number of values.
Median: middle value when sorted.
Mode: most frequent value.

experiment.description: Live Stats: Add/remove data points in a set and watch the mean, median, and mode indicators shift on a number line.

lessons.title: Basic Probability
lessons.content:
Probability measures how likely an event is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The theoretical probability of an event E is: P(E) = (number of favorable outcomes) / (total number of possible outcomes). For example, the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6.

For combined events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). If A and B are mutually exclusive (can't happen together), then P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Tree diagrams help visualize multi-step probability problems — multiply along branches and add between branches.

CSEC probability questions often involve dice, cards, colored balls in bags, or spinners. Read carefully: 'with replacement' means the probability stays the same for the second draw; 'without replacement' means it changes. Express probabilities as fractions in simplest form unless asked otherwise.
objectives: Calculate the probability of a simple event
Understand the probability scale (0 to 1)
concepts: P(E) = Number of favorable outcomes / Total outcomes.
Sum of probabilities of all possible outcomes is 1.

experiment.description: Coin Flip Lab: Simulate flipping a coin 100 or 1000 times to see how the experimental probability approaches 0.5 (theoretical).

lessons.title: Frequency Tables and Cumulative Frequency
lessons.content:
Raw data is easier to read in a frequency table. Tally each value, count the tallies and write the frequency. When the data is continuous or spread over a wide range, group it into class intervals of equal width, such as 10 — 19, 20 — 29, 30 — 39; the intervals must not overlap, and the midpoint of each interval (14.5, 24.5, 34.5) is used for calculation. Grouped data loses the individual values, so give the class interval as the measure of spread rather than pretending to know each value.

The cumulative frequency column is a running total of the frequencies: each entry is the number of items up to and including that value or interval. Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary to draw an ogive (cumulative frequency curve). From the ogive you read the median at half the total frequency, the lower quartile at one quarter and the upper quartile at three quarters, then find the interquartile range as Q3 — Q1, which describes the middle half of the data.

Worked example. If 40 students are surveyed, the median is read from the curve at cumulative frequency 20, the lower quartile at 10 and the upper quartile at 30. If these give 52, 44 and 61 marks, then the interquartile range is 61 — 44 = 17 marks and the semi-interquartile range is 8.5. For grouped data the estimated mean is Σfx ÷ Σf using the class midpoints, and the modal class is the interval with the highest frequency. Always answer in the units of the data.
objectives: Build a tally and frequency table, including grouped class intervals
Complete a cumulative frequency column and draw an ogive
Read the median, quartiles and interquartile range from a cumulative frequency curve
Estimate the mean of grouped data using class midpoints
concepts: Grouped class intervals are equal in width and must not overlap; use midpoints for calculations.
Cumulative frequency is a running total; plot it against the upper boundary.
Median at n/2, lower quartile at n/4, upper quartile at 3n/4 on the cumulative axis.
Interquartile range = Q3 — Q1; estimated mean of grouped data = Σfx/Σf.

experiment.description: Ogive Reading Match: match each statistic (median, lower quartile, upper quartile, interquartile range) to its value read from the cumulative frequency curve.

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area
lessons.content:
Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a 2D shape. For a rectangle, it is 2(length + width); for a circle, the perimeter is called the circumference and is calculated using the formula C = 2πr or C = πd. Finding the perimeter is essentially like measuring the length of a fence needed to enclose a yard.

Area is the amount of space inside the boundaries of a flat 2D object, measured in square units (like cm² or m²). The area of a rectangle is length × width, while the area of a triangle is 1/2 × base × height. For a circle, the area is πr². More complex shapes can often be broken down into these basic forms to find the total area.

CSEC problems frequently involve compound shapes, such as a rectangle with a semi-circle on top. To solve these, calculate the area of each part separately and then add them together. Accuracy with units and formulas is key. Remember: perimeter is a length (1D), while area is a surface (2D).
objectives: Calculate perimeter and area of basic shapes
Solve problems involving compound shapes
concepts: Area of rectangle = length x width.
Area of circle = πr^2.

experiment.description: Shape Flex: Resize a rectangle or circle and watch the area and perimeter values update dynamically as the dimensions change.

lessons.title: Volume and Capacity
lessons.content:
Volume is the amount of 3D space an object occupies, measured in cubic units (like cm³ or m³). For prisms (shapes with a uniform cross-section), the volume is calculated by multiplying the area of the base by the height: V = A_base × h. This applies to cubes, rectangular prisms, and cylinders.

The volume of a cylinder is therefore πr²h, since its base is a circle. Capacity refers to the amount of liquid a container can hold. While volume is the physical space occupied by the object, capacity is often expressed in liters (L) or milliliters (mL). A key conversion to remember for CSEC is that 1000 cm³ = 1 liter.

In exams, you might be asked to find the volume of a water tank or determine how many small boxes can fit into a larger container. Some problems also involve 'displacement' — when an object is submerged in water, the volume of water it displaces is equal to its own volume. Always double-check your formula and ensure your units are consistent.
objectives: Calculate the volume of prisms and cylinders
concepts: Volume = Area of base x height.

experiment.description: Water Tank: Fill different shaped 3D containers (prism, cylinder) with water to visualize how volume relates to base area and height.

lessons.title: SI Units, Conversion and Rates
lessons.content:
The International System (SI) uses base units: the metre (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, the second (s) for time and the ampere (A) for current. Prefixes scale these units — kilo means 1000, centi means 1/100, milli means 1/1000 and micro means 1/1,000,000 — so 1 km = 1000 m, 1 cm = 0.01 m and 1 mg = 0.001 g. Because area is measured in square units, 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10,000 cm²; because volume is measured in cubic units, 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³. Capacity and volume are linked: 1 cm³ = 1 mL and 1 m³ = 1000 L.

A rate compares two quantities with different units. Speed is the commonest: speed = distance ÷ time, distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed. To change km/h into m/s, multiply by 1000/3600 = 5/18; to change m/s into km/h, multiply by 18/5. A car travelling at 72 km/h covers 72 × 5/18 = 20 m each second. Density (mass ÷ volume), flow rate (litres per minute) and fuel consumption (km per litre) are handled the same way, and the unit of the answer comes from the units you divided.

Conversion questions ask you to change one unit to another by multiplying or dividing by a power of ten, and it is worth checking that the answer is sensible: a distance in metres should be much larger than in kilometres. Time needs care because it is not decimal — 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes, and 2 hours 45 minutes is 2.75 hours, not 2.45 hours. In measurement problems, copy the given values with their units, convert to a single system, then calculate, and state the unit with the final answer.
objectives: Convert between metric units of length, mass, capacity, area and volume
Use base units and prefixes correctly, including milli, centi and kilo
Calculate speed, distance and time and convert between km/h and m/s
Convert between decimal hours and hours and minutes in a real problem
concepts: SI base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere; prefixes scale by powers of ten.
Area conversions square the length factor; volume conversions cube it.
1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1 m³ = 1000 L.
km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18; m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5.

experiment.description: Unit Conversion Match: match each quantity in one metric unit to its equivalent in another, including an hours-and-minutes conversion.
